title: Luke, the Gospel and Luke-Acts
lead: The third Gospel and the longest book of the New Testament, the first half of a two-volume work whose second half is Acts, both addressed to Theophilus (Luke 1:1–4; Acts 1:1). From the late 100s the church credited it to Luke, the doctor who traveled with Paul. This page is about the book, its author and its first readers; the Gospel's stories have their own topics.

sections.b: Luke is named only three times, always in Paul's letters, always as a companion: "Luke, the dear doctor" (Colossians 4:14), a "fellow worker" (Philemon 24) and the one friend still with Paul near the end (2 Timothy 4:11). Colossians 4:10–14 seems to list him apart from the men "of the circumcision," which has led many to think he was a Gentile, though this is debated. In Acts the story suddenly says "we" in some travel scenes (Acts 16:10–17; 20:5–21:18; 27:1–28:16), as if the writer were present.
sections.refs: Colossians 4:10–14; Philemon 24; 2 Timothy 4:11; Acts 16:10–17; Acts 20:5–15; Acts 27:1–28:16

sections.b: The Gospel names no author. Irenaeus (about AD 180, Against Heresies 3.1.1) says that Luke, the companion of Paul, set down in a book the gospel Paul preached, and the Muratorian Fragment and the so-called Anti-Marcionite Prologue say the same; no ancient writer names anyone else. Many critical scholars think the author was an unknown Gentile Christian of the next generation who used the "we" style to join his sources or to mark travel narrative. Others, including Joseph Fitzmyer, accept that the companion of Paul wrote both books. The old argument that Luke's vocabulary is especially medical (W. K. Hobart, 1882) was answered by Henry Cadbury, who showed that other educated Greek writers used the same words.

Most scholars date the Gospel to about AD 80–90, after Mark and after the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70, which Luke 19:43–44 and Luke 21:20–24 seem to describe. Some date it before 70, because Acts ends with Paul still alive in Rome about AD 62; a few (Richard Pervo, Joseph Tyson) place Luke-Acts in the early 100s. The place is unknown; the old prologue names Achaia (Greece), and Antioch, Rome and Asia Minor are also proposed. The book is written for Theophilus, "most excellent," and through him for Christians, most of them probably Gentiles, who needed to know that what they had been taught was solid (Luke 1:4).

About AD 140 Marcion of Sinope, who taught that the Father of Jesus was not the God of Israel, used a shorter Gospel close to Luke, without chapters 1–2 and other passages. Irenaeus and Tertullian (Against Marcion 4) said he cut Luke down. A minority of recent scholars (Matthias Klinghardt, Jason BeDuhn) argue that Marcion's Gospel came first and that our Luke expanded it. Most specialists, including Dieter Roth, who reconstructed Marcion's text from the church fathers' quotations, still hold that Marcion edited Luke.

Among the four living creatures of Ezekiel 1:10 and Revelation 4:7, Luke is usually given the ox or calf, because his Gospel opens with a priest serving in the temple, where oxen were sacrificed. A story attributed to Theodore the Reader (500s), preserved only in later excerpts whose authenticity is debated, said Luke painted the earliest icon of Mary, and several icons were later credited to him; historians treat this as legend, though it made Luke the patron saint of painters. His feast is October 18 in both East and West.
